world_behind.title: A chapter that starts mid-sentence
world_behind.text: The previous chapter ended with men falling by the sword and a city sitting on the ground. This one opens with the consequence: seven women to one man. The chapter number falls in the middle of a single movement, and reading across the break restores a scene the division interrupts.

world_behind.title: Why seven women want a name
world_behind.text: Their offer is to feed and clothe themselves, asking only "let us be called by thy name" (v. 1). Marriage in that world carried legal standing, inheritance, and protection; an unmarried woman without sons had none of it. The war has not only killed men, it has stranded the survivors outside the structures that made life possible.

world_behind.title: Three chapters, one oracle
world_behind.text: Isaiah 2 through 4 work as a single movement: a mountain promised, a society taken apart, and then a cleansed remnant under a covering. Nephi copied all three in order and put none of his own words between them, which suggests he read them as one piece.

world_behind.title: Filth and blood as ritual terms
world_behind.text: Verse 4 uses the vocabulary of temple purification rather than of hygiene. What is washed away belongs to Zion's daughters, the same women itemized in the previous chapter, and what is purged is bloodguilt. The city is being cleaned the way a sanctuary is cleaned before it can be used.

world_behind.title: Assemblies as well as houses
world_behind.text: Verse 5 covers two things: the dwelling-places and "her assemblies" (v. 5). The word points at the appointed gatherings of Israel's calendar, the feasts and holy convocations, which were the occasions when a scattered population became visibly one people. Both the private address and the public occasion are put under the same covering.

world_behind.title: Shade and shelter in a hot country
world_behind.text: The last verse names heat, storm, and rain, in that order, the order of a Judean year's real dangers. A tabernacle for shade and a covert from rain are ordinary structures. The promise is not that the weather stops but that the covering holds.

words.text: "To take away our reproach" (v. 1): reproach is a shame that comes from a situation rather than from a sin, and nothing in the verse accuses these women of anything. The other two places this record uses the word are Isaiah as well, and they work the same way: a reproach of men that the law-keeping are told not to fear (2 Ne. 8:7), and a reproach of widowhood that will not be remembered (3 Ne. 22:4). What the word names is exposure, and that is why a name can lift it.

A shoot growing out of a stump or root, and in the prophets a standard figure for a descendant who continues a line that looked finished. Treated at 2 Nephi 3:5. Jeremiah promises to raise "a righteous Branch" (Jer. 23:5) for David, and Isaiah will use the related rod-out-of-a-stem image later in this block. The record uses the same word in another sense for Joseph's posterity, so the two have to be kept apart: this branch is a person, that one is a people. Either way the word carries smallness and survival together, which is why it suits a chapter about a remnant.

Pleasing to look at, in a plain and fitting way. The word appears twice in this record and sixteen times in the King James Bible. Here it describes the fruit of the earth for those who escaped, and the other use in the record is a congregation that wore no costly apparel and was still "neat and comely" (Alma 1:27). Both attach the word to something modest that looks right.

A cleaning word with a legal edge: to remove guilt as well as residue. What is purged here is "the blood of Jerusalem" (v. 4), the accumulated liability of violence done in the city. The verb assumes the stain is real and removable, and God is the one who does the removing.

"The Lord will create upon every dwelling-place of mount Zion" (v. 5): the verb is the Genesis one (Gen. 1:1, 27), used there of heavens and earth and man, and here it is spent on cloud, smoke, and firelight over rooftops. Shelter in this verse is not merely provided, it is made, and by the maker of everything else.

spans.text: The Lord will create upon every dwelling-place of mount Zion

words.text: A tabernacle is a tent, something pitched and struck again, so the word the chapter picks for its shelter names a structure that moves. Israel's own booths at the harvest feast were branches, put up for a week. This record's other uses of the word go a different direction, toward the body: a Lord who will "dwell in a tabernacle of clay" (Mosiah 3:5), and the mortal tabernacle Alma expects him to live in (Alma 7:8). In each case the tent is the temporary thing and what it houses is not.

phrases.term: They that are left in Zion
phrases.text: The KJV describes an individual twice: "he that is left in Zion, and he that remaineth in Jerusalem" (Isa. 4:3). This reading makes both plural. A promise about one surviving man becomes a promise about a surviving group. That is the difference between a token and a remnant, and the rest of the chapter is about a community.

phrases.term: Written among the living in Jerusalem
phrases.text: A register of citizens, and a term the scriptures keep reaching for. The psalmist asks that his enemies be "blotted out of the book of the living" (Ps. 69:28); Alma will promise that the names of the righteous are written in the book of life. Whether Isaiah means a civic roll or a heavenly one, the survivors are described as listed somewhere, by name, which is a specific kind of comfort.

phrases.term: By the spirit of judgment and by the spirit of burning
phrases.text: The two instruments of the cleaning, and neither is gentle. Judgment sorts and fire consumes, and both are called spirit, which keeps them from being read as merely political events. The verse gives the method for the promise: this is how the filth of the previous chapter gets washed away, and there is no version of it that avoids heat.

phrases.term: A cloud and smoke by day
phrases.text: The exodus signs, quoted in their familiar order. Israel followed "a pillar of a cloud" (Ex. 13:21) out of Egypt, and the promise here is that the same presence returns, this time stationary and multiplied over every house. Nephi's people had their own wilderness travel behind them and a compass instead of a pillar; the image would not have been an antique to them.

phrases.term: Upon all the glory of Zion shall be a defence
phrases.text: The KJV promises a defence "upon all the glory" (Isa. 4:5), leaving the glory unspecified. Two added words attach it to Zion. The line then says something more pointed: the city's glory is what needs guarding, and it is guarded by a covering rather than by walls or soldiers, neither of which the previous chapter left standing.

phrases.term: A covert from storm and from rain
phrases.text: The chapter's last promise is the smallest one in it. A covert is a thicket or an overhang, somewhere to get out of the weather, and it closes a run of increasingly ordinary shelters: tabernacle, shadow, place of refuge, covert. After the branch, the holy remnant, the purging fire, and the pillar of cloud, the closing image is a place to stand out of the rain, something a frightened person can picture without effort.

verses.label: v. 1
verses.title: The chapter opens mid-sentence from the one before it
verses.text: The seven women taking hold of one man continue directly out of the judgment on the daughters of Zion in 2 Nephi 13, and the chapter break falls inside the thought. The variants leave the seam alone: verse 1 is one of only two here they do not touch.

verses.label: v. 1–6
verses.title: Two thirds of a six-verse chapter is revised
verses.text: Isaiah 4 is the shortest chapter in the block, and the variants touch two thirds of it: four deletions, four replacements, two insertions. Measured against the whole family this is a high rate, sixty-seven per cent, placing a six-verse chapter near 2 Nephi 12 and 13 for density of change.

verses.label: v. 2
verses.title: A promise loses its auxiliary and changes its preposition
verses.text: Isaiah has "the branch of the Lord shall be beautiful and glorious"; here the verb is gone and the fruit of the earth is excellent and comely to them that are escaped, rather than for them. What was stated as a future becomes a description, and the beneficiaries are given a different relation to it.

verses.label: v. 3
verses.title: Two long relative clauses collapse into verbs
verses.text: Isaiah reads "he that is left in Zion, and he that remaineth in Jerusalem." The variants turn both into plain plurals, are and remain, and add a they. Nine words of King James circumlocution become four, and the sentence stops naming an individual and starts naming a group.

verses.label: v. 5
verses.title: Zion is named where Isaiah left it implied
verses.text: Isaiah's verse promises a cloud and smoke by day and a flaming fire by night "upon every dwelling place of mount Zion." Here two words are inserted so that the dwelling place is explicitly of Zion. It is the chapter's only substantive insertion, and it lands on the one noun that had been left general.

chapter.title: Six verses that answer twenty-six
chapter.text: Nearly every promise here reverses a specific loss from the chapter before it. The women who were itemized are washed; the city that sat on the ground is covered; the men who fell leave seven women to a man. The two chapters are one argument, and the numbering hides it.

chapter.title: The cleansing is not optional or painless
chapter.text: The instruments are judgment and burning, and they are applied to the covenant city rather than to its enemies. A reader looking for a comfortable chapter after chapter 13 gets comfort, but only on the far side of a fire that is described before the shelter is.

chapter.title: Glory and shelter, in that order
chapter.text: Six verses run from "the branch of the Lord be beautiful and glorious" at verse 2 to "a covert from storm and from rain" at verse 6. In between stand a washing, a burning, a cloud, a flaming fire, and a defence. The final item is the smallest and the only one a person could shelter under. The same descent from glory to shelter closes 2 Nephi 8 with a cup taken from the hand, and closes Alma 34 with a plain instruction to pray in the fields.

chapter.title: The remnant is plural here
chapter.text: The variant at verse 3 turns two singular survivors into groups. In a block that Nephi selected for a scattered family on an island, the difference is not incidental: what is promised is a people left, not a lone survivor, and his own colony is a small group of exactly that kind.

chapter.title: The exodus keeps returning
chapter.text: Verse 5 supplies "a cloud and smoke by day and the shining of a flaming fire by night" and verse 6 "a tabernacle for a shadow in the daytime from the heat." All three items come from Exodus 13:21 and Exodus 40:34–38, and none is explained here. This is the first exodus vocabulary in the copied block, and the record's own writers use the same figures of their own crossing at 1 Nephi 17:23–31 and Alma 36:28.

chapter.title: A short chapter carrying the block's promise
chapter.text: Chapters 12 and 13 are almost entirely judgment. This one holds nearly all of the consolation in the block's opening movement, and it is the shortest of the three. The proportion is worth noticing before the longer oracles that follow, since Isaiah's ratio of warning to promise rarely favors promise by length.

applications.title: Read across the break
applications.text: Take the chapter division you are most used to stopping at in your own study and read straight through it once, out loud. Chapter numbers were added long after these words were spoken, and the seam between 13 and 14 hides a promise attached to a disaster.

applications.title: Check what you want to be called
applications.text: Seven women offered to feed and clothe themselves and asked only for a name. Ask what standing you are currently seeking, whose name you want attached to yours, and whether the answer would embarrass you if said plainly.

applications.title: Read the verse that follows the title
applications.text: They that are left in Zion shall be called holy, and the next sentence says when: after the Lord has washed away the filth of the daughters of Zion and purged the blood of Jerusalem. The name arrives before its condition, which is how names usually arrive; you get called something and afterward learn what it costs. When you take on a title, a calling, a role, a family reputation, read the following verse and do the part that has to happen for the name to become true.

applications.title: Let the cleansing be God's verb
applications.text: Every action in the washing belongs to the Lord. Identify the thing about yourself you have been trying hardest to scrub, and spend a week asking for it to be washed.

applications.title: Put the pillar over the house
applications.text: The exodus signs land on dwellings here. Choose one practice that makes your home rather than your meetinghouse the place where God is expected, and start it this week.

applications.title: Name your shelter honestly
applications.text: The chapter's final promise is shade and a roof. Write down what you are actually asking God for right now, and see whether you are asking for the storm to stop or for somewhere to stand in it.

questions.text: What am I willing to provide for myself, and what do I still need to be given by someone else?
Where have I seen something beautiful grow out of a stump I had written off?
If a roll of the living were kept by name, what would I want written next to mine?
What in me is being purged right now by judgment or by burning, and am I calling it something else?
Does the presence of God in my life feel national and distant, or is it over my own dwelling?
When the storm comes, where do I actually go first?
